text.p: *** BIRTHDAYS ***
Author of the first Australian novel, Henry Savey, was born in England in 1791. He was convicted of forgery and transported to Hobart where he wrote "Qintus Serviton".
English poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, who drowned at the age of 30, was born in 1792.
Scottish composer and entertainer Sir Harry Lauder, who had a hit with "Roamin' In The Gloamin'", was born in 1870.
The Queen Mother, Queen Elizabeth, was born Lady Elizabeth Bowes-Lyon at Glamis Castle in Scotland in 1900.
American singer Franki Ford, who began his career while still at school, was born in 1939. His biggest hit was "Sea Cruise" in 1959. He was considered a synthesis of Elvis Presley and Ricky Nelson.

New Zealand labour politician and former prime minister David Russell Lange was born in 1942. During his time as leader of the country (1984-89) he created controversy over his refusal to allow nuclear-armed American warships to dock in New Zealand. British keyboard player with the 'Fortunes' David Carr was born in 1943.
Guitarist, singer and songwriter Paul Reynolds, from 'A Flock of Seagulls', was born in 1962.
*** EVENTS ***

1875: Famous fairy tale writer, Hans Christian Andersen, died at the age of 70. Andersen was born into poverty, the son of a cobbler. His first book of fairy tales in 1835 was a bestseller throughout the world.
1901: A major gold discovery was made in the Rand district in South Africa.
1910: In Sydney, authorities considered building a tunnel under the harbour, linking the north and south of the city by rail.

1914: Britain declared war on Germany after the Germans failed to agree to a withdrawal from Belgium. The British House of Commons was filled with loud cheers as the Prime Minister Herbert Asquith detailed the ultimatum, calling on Germany to respect the neutrality of Belgium. The subsequent declaration of war was met by cheering crowds surging through London streets singing the national anthem.
1940: The Italians invaded British Somaliland in East Africa.
1954: Britain's first supersonic fighter plane, the P-1 English Electric Lighting, made its maiden flight.

1978: Britain's former liberal leader Jeremy Thorpe appeared in court, denying having had a homosexual affair, and then plotting to have his lover killed. Thorpe and three other men were accused of conspiring to kill Norman Scott, a male model.
Thorpe lost his seat at the 1979 election, and two months later he was found not guilty of plotting a murder.

1983: Queensland Liberal Welfare Services Minister Terry White crossed the floor of parliament and voted with Labor. The two conservative parties, the liberals and the nationals, were still involved in negotiations ten years later, to mend the rift that developed in the 1980's.
1984: Australia won three gold medals at the Los Angeles Olympics. The medallists were Glynis Nunn on the athletics track, Jon Sieben in the pool and at the veladrome, the pursuit cycling team.
1989: At his first news conference, Japan's new emperor Akihito defended the right of people to accuse his father, Hirohito, of war time atrocities.
1990: In London, more than 2,000 well-wishers gathered outside Clarence House to cheer the Queen Mother on her 90th birthday.

1990: A multi-million dollar counterfeiting ring was smashed after a man was arrested in London. He had printing plates and enough security paper to print counterfeit money to the value of 25 million dollars.
1990: Iraq installed a puppet government in Kuwait and set up a new People's Army.
1990: The president of the British Women Pilot's association, Naomi Christie, celebrated her 79th birthday with a flight with a difference. She stood on the top of a Tiger Moth as it flew.
